meaning: Network Attached Storage. Our Synology NAS is a file server on the office network. It stores shared files and runs the packages in this guide.
DiskStation Manager, the operating system of the NAS. You sign in to DSM in a web browser to open apps such as File Station.
The app store inside DSM. IT installs, updates and removes packages from here.
An app or service installed on the NAS from Package Center.
A top-level folder on the NAS, for example "Sales" or "Finance". IT decides who can read or change each one.
Your username and password for the NAS. It may be the same as your Windows or domain sign-in.
Synology's relay service. It lets Synology apps reach our NAS from outside the office without opening ports on the router.
An encrypted tunnel from your laptop to the office network, so you can use internal services from home or a regional office.
The Windows file-sharing protocol. It lets you open a NAS shared folder as a network drive in Windows, for example drive Z.
A way to open NAS files over the web (HTTP/HTTPS). Some apps and mobile file managers use it.
A read-only, point-in-time copy of a shared folder. Used to restore files quickly after a mistake or a ransomware attack.
A scheduled job that copies data somewhere else: another NAS, a USB drive or a cloud service.
Keep 3 copies of important data, on 2 different types of storage, with 1 copy offsite.
Ways of combining disks so the NAS keeps working when one disk fails. RAID is not a backup: deleted or encrypted files are lost on every disk at once.
A storage area built from the NAS disks. Shared folders live on volumes.
Signing in with your password plus a second check, such as an approval on your phone or a security key.
Central user directories. They let one username and password work across many systems.
A packaged app that runs isolated on the NAS through Container Manager (Docker).
Some packages need paid licences for extra users, mailboxes, cameras or features.
Software that no longer gets security fixes. It should be upgraded or removed.
